Tropical Storm Bertha is expected to bring heavy rain, flooding along the Gulf Coast
Tropical Storm Bertha strengthened in the Gulf of Mexico on Tuesday but was expected to weaken as it chugs closer to the U.S., potentially bringing coastal flooding and heavy rain from the Florida Panhandle to Louisiana.
Those areas along the northern Gulf Coast were under a tropical storm warning through Wednesday and could see heavy rain and flooding into Thursday morning, the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said Tuesday. New Orleans was under a tropical storm watch.
The storm was about 90 miles (145 kilometers) south-southwest of Panama City, Florida, and 125 miles (200 kilometers) southeast of Mobile, Alabama, and moving slowly with maximum sustained winds of 60 mph (95 kph), the hurricane center said Tuesday. Gradual weakening was forecast through Friday.
Bertha was forecast to make landfall Wednesday night somewhere in the coastal and lightly populated part of Louisiana southeast of New Orleans, said Michael Buchanan, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Louisiana.
Wind will be biggest threat there, he said.
Authorities open sites to distribute sandbags
Authorities in Mississippi, Louisiana and Florida opened sites to provide sandbags to residents while red flag warnings were posted along some beaches advising swimmers about the dangers of rip tides.
Up and down the coast, double red flags signaled that Gulf waters were closed for swimming.
Beaches near Pensacola, Florida, were mostly deserted except for tourists venturing out to take photos of the pounding surf.
“For locals, this is just another storm,” said Candice Henderson, manager of the Crab Trap, a beachside restaurant that was packed Tuesday on Pensacola’s Perdido Key. “When you’re on vacation and its raining, you either shop or you go out to eat.”
The storm was expected to weaken as it moves along the coast, said Jamie Rhome of the hurricane center. It’s possible that the worst of the storm will stay offshore, he said Tuesday.
Bertha was expected to weaken further as it pushes into Texas, forecasters said.
Forecasts called for as much as 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 centimeters) of rain from western Florida to the southern Louisiana coastline, with higher amounts in some scattered areas.
That could cause flash flooding in some urban areas.
Authorities also advised that areas in Louisiana from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Alabama-Mississippi state line could see storm surges of up to 4 feet (1.2 meters). Parts of Florida and Alabama could see smaller surges.
Bertha is the second tropical storm of the Atlantic hurricane season
Bertha is the second tropical storm of the Atlantic hurricane season. Tropical Storm Arthur last month brought heavy rainfall to the southeastern U.S.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration expects this year to see a below-average Atlantic hurricane season although that doesn’t eliminate the chances of a catastrophic storm.
Bertha could dump heavy rain on coastal areas of Mississippi that are still recovering from flooding brought by Arthur that destroyed and damaged homes in June.
“Because of that, people are definitely paying attention, or at least you would hope so,” said Jeff Clark, a spokesperson for Mississippi’s Harrison County, where six sites were open for sandbag distribution.
So far, there hasn’t been a need to open any shelters or order evacuations, Clark said on Tuesday.
Hurricane Fausto churns in the Pacific
In the eastern Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Fausto churned far from Mexico’s Baja California peninsula and posed no threat to land, the hurricane center said.
Fausto gained hurricane status Monday night. It was about 735 miles (1,185 kilometers) southwest of the southern tip of Baja California, had top sustained winds of 75 mph (120 kph) and was moving northwest at 12 mph (19 kph).
The storm was expected to strengthen Tuesday and Wednesday. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect, though ocean swells generated by the storm could cause life-threatening surf and rip tide conditions on the Baja California coast, the center said.

Tropical Storm Bertha Update: CenterPoint Energy Continues to Prepare for Potential Impacts Across Greater Houston Area
Additional CenterPoint preparations underway as the hottest temperatures of the year so far may impact equipment in some areas on Tuesday and Wednesday ahead of any potential tropical impacts later in the week
Key actions taken to date: activating Emergency Operations Center, mobilizing approximately 1,050 frontline workers with an additional 1,100 available if needed, conducting outreach to customers, and coordinating with local emergency response partners
HOUSTON — July 21, 2026 — As part of its overall response to prepare for the potential impacts of now Tropical Storm Bertha as well as the hottest temperatures of the year so far, CenterPoint Energy has activated its Emergency Operations Center as of Monday, July 20th at 12:00 PM CT. CenterPoint continues to take a series of readiness actions, including closely monitoring weather conditions and proactively mobilizing approximately 1,050 frontline personnel to respond to storm-related outages, conducting outreach to customers, and coordinating with local officials and emergency response partners. Additionally, the company has secured an additional 1,100 contractors to help support restoration efforts, if needed.
Based on current weather forecasts, the National Hurricane Center predicts Tropical Storm Bertha will weaken upon approach to the southeast TX coastline – arriving on Friday as a Tropical Depression or Post-Tropical area of low pressure. Minimal impacts include the potential for wind gusts of mainly 25-35mph, and rain totals of mainly 1-2″ or below from isolated thunderstorms as most of the storm’s impacts are displaced on the south side over open Gulf waters. To prepare for potential impacts of now Tropical Storm Bertha, CenterPoint Energy is once again urging all customers to immediately enroll in Power Alert Service® to receive important updates about their gas and electric service via text, email or phone calls, including service outages and estimated restoration times.
“Re-affirming our all-hazards approach to emergency preparedness, our team continues to take critical actions to prepare for the both the current Tropical Storm Bertha in the Gulf as well as the hottest temperatures of the season, including activating our Emergency Operations Center and mobilizing more than 1,050 frontline crew members to prepare for the impacts of these weather events. We are also in close contact with our emergency partners to be ready to respond and restore power safely and as quickly as possible. Finally, we are urging our customers and their families to take steps to stay safe, including signing up for Power Alert Service to get the latest updates on outages and restoration times,” said Nathan Brownell, CenterPoint Energy’s Vice President, Resilience and Capital Delivery and Incident Commander.
Actions CenterPoint Energy is Taking to Respond
As part of its continued preparedness efforts, CenterPoint Energy is taking the following actions to prepare for and respond to the potential impacts of Tropical Storm Bertha for its Greater Houston area customers:
- Activated Emergency Operations Center: Coordinating local preparedness and response efforts.
- Actively monitoring weather: Closely monitoring National Hurricane Center forecasts and evolving weather conditions that could impact Texas.
- Secured crews and equipment: Additional crews and equipment to quickly respond to potential storm impacts once conditions have cleared.
- Communicating with customers: Communicating directly to customers via email, phone, text or other channels to keep them informed and prepared, with over 980,000 communications sent to date.
- Promoting Power Alert Service®: Urging customers to sign up for Power Alert Service® to receive important updates about their gas and electric service via phone call, text or email, including outage details and estimated restoration times.
- Conducting outreach to critical care customers: Reaching out to identified Critical Care Residential and Chronic Condition Residential electric customers by email, phone and/or text to make them aware of the potential for storm-related outages.
- Coordinating with government officials: Providing regular updates to federal, state, county and city officials regarding preparedness activities.
Emergency Communications: Sign Up for Power Alert Service®
To receive important updates about gas and electric service via phone call, text or email, including outage details and estimated restoration times, CenterPoint Energy customers are strongly encouraged to enroll in Power Alert Service®. As part of CenterPoint Energy’s overall emergency communications efforts, customers can stay up to date on local outages with its cloud-based Outage Tracker, available in English and Spanish, which allows customers to see outages and restoration times by county, city and zip code.
Emergency Preparations: What Customers Can Do to Stay Safe
To help ensure their safety, CenterPoint Energy is encouraging all its customers and their families to follow their emergency plan during this event. Customers can find specific safety tips to help them prepare at CenterPointEnergy.com/ActionCenter.

sources.news_title: Mississippi Gulf Coast Under Storm Surge Watch as Tropical Storm Bertha Nears
sources.text:
NEW ORLEANS (AP) — The Mississippi Gulf Coast is now under a storm surge watch as Tropical Storm Bertha nears land. The storm strengthened in the Gulf of Mexico and was moving slowly toward the Gulf Coast on Tuesday morning, causing a tropical storm warning and storm surge watches across several states, forecasters said.
The storm was about 110 miles (177 kilometers) south of Panama City, Florida, and 170 miles (274 kilometers) southeast of Mobile, Alabama, and moving northwest at 5 mph (8 kph) with maximum sustained winds of 50 mph (80 kph), the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said Tuesday morning.
The wind speed increased by 10 mph (16 kph) since Bertha formed Monday night. A tropical storm warning, meaning the conditions are expected within the warning area within 36 hours, was in effect early Tuesday from the Florida and Alabama border, across the Mississippi Gulf Coast and to the Jefferson and Plaquemines parish line in Louisiana.
A storm surge watch, indicating rising, possible life-threatening water moving inland from the coast within 48 hours, was issued from the Alabama and Florida border to the mouth of the Mississippi River, the hurricane center reported.
Bertha Is Expected to Stay Near or Along the Gulf Coast
Bertha is the second tropical storm of the Atlantic hurricane season after Tropical Storm Arthur brought heavy rainfall to the southeastern U.S. in June.
The storm was expected to stay near or along the northern Gulf Coast this week, dropping heavy rain on coastal areas of Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana while pushing west toward Texas.
Potentially life-threatening storm surges of up to 4 feet (1.2 meters) are possible in portions of Mississippi, Louisiana, Alabama and Florida, the hurricane center said, warning Bertha could spin off an isolated tornado or two over the Florida Big Bend region. The Mississippi Gulf Coast could experience wind speeds between 40 and 60 mph, forecasters say.
Areas of flash flooding also will be possible through Friday along the coast from western Florida to middle Texas, forecasters said, adding that rainfall could total 3 to 5 inches (7 to 12 centimeters) along the Louisiana coastline, with higher amounts in some scattered areas.
Red flags on the beach at Orange Beach, Alabama, cautioned swimmers about high surf and currents. In Escambia County, Florida, emergency officials offered sand for people living in flood-prone areas to use for sandbags.
Hurricane Fausto Churns in the Pacific
In the eastern Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Fausto churned far from Mexico’s Baja California peninsula and posed no threat to land, the hurricane center said.
Fausto gained hurricane status Monday night. It was about 740 miles (1,191 kilometers) southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula, had top sustained winds of 80 mph (129 kph) and was moving northwest at 12 mph (19 kph).
The storm was expected to strengthen Tuesday and Wednesday. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect, though ocean swells generated by the storm could cause life-threatening surf and rip tide conditions on the Baja California coast, the center said.
Mississippi Free Press News Editor Ashton Pittman contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Tropical Storm Bertha strengthens as warnings extend along Gulf Coast, NHC says
sources.text:
Tropical Storm Bertha strengthened Tuesday as it moved closer to the Gulf Coast and the National Hurricane Center extended tropical storm warnings into Florida.
As of the NHC’s 2 p.m. advisory, the center of Bertha was located about 90 miles southwest of Panama City and 125 miles southeast of Mobile, Alabama, moving northwest at 5 mph with maximum sustained winds of 60 mph and higher gusts.
Tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 90 miles from Bertha’s center. A National Ocean Service station in Panama City Beach reported sustained winds of 42 mph and a gust of 49 mph after noon as tropical-storm conditions began lashing the Florida Panhandle.
“Bertha is expected to turn toward the west-northwest and west later today and tonight. Then, a continued westward motion is forecast through the middle of the week,” said NHC senior hurricane specialist Brad Reinhart. “On the forecast track, Bertha will move near or along the northern Gulf Coast during the next several days.”
The NHC extended a tropical storm warning to include seven Florida counties from the Florida-Alabama border east to the Bay-Gulf County line. The warning also extends west from the Florida-Alabama border to the Terrebonne/Lafourche Parish Line in Louisiana.
A tropical storm watch is in effect for west of the Terrebonne/Lafourche Parish Line to the Vermilion/Cameron Parish Line and for metropolitan New Orleans, Lake Pontchartrain and Lake Maurepas.
A storm surge warning that had been in place for parts of the Gulf Coast was discontinued, but the National Weather Service has issued flood warning for parts of the southeastern Louisiana and Mississippi coastline.
Tropical Storm Bertha tracking map: Here’s the latest forecast path
What had been the second tropical depression of the Atlantic hurricane season spun into a named storm by 8 p.m. Monday with 40 mph winds, but had picked up steam by 11 p.m. and intensified further through Tuesday morning.
Reinhart said models show the system is likely at its peak intensity, and should begin to gradually weaken over the next few days.
“Bertha remains an asymmetric tropical storm, with most of the rainfall and the strongest winds occurring to the south and east of the center,” he said. “Strong northeasterly vertical wind shear over Bertha is forecast to persist today and tonight, which should make it difficult for Bertha to strengthen much more.”
Tropical-storm conditions are expected within the warning area later Tuesday and into Wednesday while conditions are possible in the watch area in Louisiana on Wednesday.
A storm surge of 1-3 feet could hit the Florida coast from Indian Pass to the Aucilla River while surge could hit 2-4 feet from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Mississippi-Alabama border, and 1-3 feet from that border to the Alabama-Florida border, Lake Pontchartrain and from the Vermilion/Cameron Parish line in Louisiana to the mouth of the Mississippi River.
In addition, rainfall of 2-4 inches through Thursday, with some areas seeing up to 6 inches, is forecast along the Gulf Coast and adjacent inland locations from western Florida into southern Louisiana, including southern portions ofAlabama and Mississippi, with a threat of flash flooding.
Swells along the coast could cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions.
Short-lived Tropical Storm Arthur was the season’s first named storm that developed in the Gulf and brought floods to Texas and Louisiana in June.
Cristobal is the next name on the hurricane season list followed by Dolly.
The season officially began June 1 and runs through Nov. 30. The height of hurricane season runs from mid-August into October.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration expects this season to be below normal with the official forecast released in late May calling for 8-14 named storms, of which 3-6 would become hurricanes. Of those, 1-3 would become major hurricanes reaching Category 3 status or above.
An average season has 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes.

sources.news_title: Why This Week Could Be Extra Rainy in Disney World
sources.text:
The second named storm of this year’s Atlantic hurricane season has now strengthened from a tropical depression into a tropical storm.
This year’s storm season is expected to bring fewer storms than normal, but that doesn’t mean we don’t need to pay attention to the ones that do happen. Right now, we’ve got our eye on Tropical Storm Bertha — here’s the latest updates you need to know.
According to USA Today, Tropical Storm Bertha strengthened from a depression on July 20th when the storm was “stationary.” As of 10 PM that night, the storm was located 140 miles south of Panama City, Florida, and about 215 miles southeast of Mobile, Alabama. The storm currently has maximum sustained winds of 40 miles per hour.
The storm is expected to arrive closer to land at 1 PM on Wednesday, and make actual landfall around 1 AM Thursday morning in Louisiana. Tropical storm watches are in effect all along the Gulf coast, as the National Hurricane Center has warned that strong winds, heavy rain and dangerous surf conditions could develop into today, July 21st. A storm surge watch is also in effect from the Alabama-Florida border to the mouth of the Mississippi River.
This storm won’t affect Orlando intensely, other than potentially some rain and wind from the outer bands, but as the storm continues to move closer to Texas, the threat in Orlando will dissipate. The storm is expected to drop around 2-4 inches of rain “with locally higher totals around 8 inches through Friday along the Gulf Coast and adjacent inland locations from western Florida to the Middle Texas Coast, including southern portions of Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana.” Flooding could be made worse due to hard, dense, dry soil, so it’s advised you stay alert.

A tropical storm watch was upgraded to a tropical storm warning from the Bay/Gulf County line in Florida westward to the Florida/Alabama border. Some Florida impacts are predicted from Bertha, including some rain, gusty winds and dangerous surf. Elsewhere, the tropics were quiet as of 5 p.m. July 21. The National Hurricane Center wasn't highlighting any disturbances on its tropical outlook map, but is watching three tropical waves in the Atlantic basin, including one in the Caribbean.

When is hurricane season in Florida?
The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June 1 through Nov. 30.
Ninety-seven percent of tropical cyclone activity occurs during this time period, NOAA said.
➤ Hurricane Center testing new cone: What's changing this season?
The Atlantic basin includes the northern Atlantic Ocean, Caribbean Sea and Gulf of America, as the Gulf of Mexico is now known in the U.S. per an order from President Trump. NOAA and the National Hurricane Center are now using Gulf of America on its maps and in its advisories.

Special note on the NHC cone: The forecast track shows the most likely path of the center of the storm. It does not illustrate the full width of the storm or its impacts, and the center of the storm could travel outside the cone. Special note about spaghetti models: Illustrations include an array of forecast tools and models, and not all are created equal. The Hurricane Center uses only the top four or five highest performing models to help make its forecasts.
What impacts can Florida expect from Tropical Storm Bertha?
"Overall, Bertha is a low-grade tropical threat to North Florida and the Central Gulf Coast, and overall won’t be much different from a normal summer mix of sun and rain away from the immediate coast," said Dr. Ryan Truchelut, chief meteorologist at WeatherTiger, who works with the USA TODAY Network.
Tropical storm conditions were spreading westward in the Florida Panhandle as of 5 p.m., July 21, according to the National Hurricane Center.
Bertha is expected to produce total rainfall amounts of 2 to 4 inches with isolated higher totals around 6 inches through July 23 along the central Gulf Coast from western Florida into southern Louisiana, the National Hurricane Center said.
Areas of flash flooding will be possible through July 23 along the Gulf Coast and adjacent inland locations from the Florida Big Bend region to southern Louisiana, although the heaviest rain is forecast to remain over the Gulf, the National Weather Service Mobile said.
"The immediate coast from Cedar Key to Mobile could see peak gusts of low-end tropical-storm force (40-50 mph) in squally bands," Truchelut said.
"For inland areas of the Panhandle, a few localized gusts into the low-end tropical storm range are possible in the heaviest bands, but Bertha will not be a widespread wind damage event."
Swells generated by Bertha are affecting portions of the Gulf coast of Florida and will continue to spread westward over the next few days. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions.
There's a high risk of rip currents along the northern Gulf Coast, with surf building throughout the day and breakers of 8-11 feet late tonight through Wednesday night, the National Weather Service Mobile said.

National Hurricane Center tracking 3 tropical waves
The National Hurricane Center is watching three tropical waves in the Atlantic basin, as of 8 a.m. July 21:
- An eastern Atlantic tropical wave is just west of the Cabo Verde Islands along 29W from 09N to 19W, moving west at 11 to 17 mph.
- A central Atlantic tropical wave is its axis along 47W from 09N to 23N, moving west at around 17 mph.
- A tropical wave over the far southwestern Caribbean is moving into central America along 83W, S of 18N. It is moving west at around 11 mph.
What is a tropical wave?
"Tropical waves are clusters of showers and thunderstorms that act as the seedlings for many tropical storms throughout the Atlantic season," said Alex DaSilva, AccuWeather lead hurricane expert, via email.
“There are about 60 tropical waves that move across the Atlantic each year, and roughly 10 percent to 15 percent of them develop into a tropical system. That’s about one in seven.
"Tropical waves are important because they contribute to about 80 percent of all major hurricanes."
A major hurricane is a storm that is a Category 3 or stronger, with maximum sustained winds of at least 111 mph.
How many tropical storms, hurricanes are in a typical season?
The 30-year average, from 1991 to 2020, is for 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes.

sources.text:
FPREN | By Irene Sans
The National Hurricane Center has upgraded Tropical Depression Two to Tropical Storm Bertha after NOAA Hurricane Hunters found the system had strengthened during Monday afternoon. Bertha now has maximum sustained winds of 40 mph, is moving west-northwest at 5 mph, and has a minimum central pressure of 1004 mb.
Although Bertha has strengthened into a tropical storm, its overall organization remains limited. Dry air wrapping into the circulation and strong wind shear of around 25 knots (and increasing over its east and northeast) are expected to prevent rapid intensification as the storm drifts slowly across the northeastern Gulf of Mexico. Hurricane Hunters also observed the center wobbling throughout the day as the storm remains trapped between two areas of high pressure, resulting in weak steering currents and an erratic motion. Additional reconnaissance flights are scheduled through Wednesday, and slight adjustments to the forecast track remain possible.
Bertha is expected to continue moving very slowly through Tuesday before gradually turning more westward later this week. The National Hurricane Center continues to forecast a track toward southeastern Louisiana on Wednesday, although the cone of uncertainty still allows for the center to remain offshore. If Bertha spends more time over the warm Gulf waters, some additional strengthening is possible despite the unfavorable environment.
Tropical Storm Watch and Storm Surge Watch in effect for parts of the Panhandle.
Tropical Storm Watches remain in effect from the Florida Panhandle westward to Plaquemines Parish, Louisiana, with a Storm Surge Watch extending from the Alabama-Florida border to the mouth of the Mississippi River. Tropical-storm-force winds are expected to begin affecting the western Florida Panhandle Monday night, especially from Panama City Beach to Pensacola, before spreading along the Mississippi and Alabama coasts on Tuesday. By Tuesday night, stronger wind gusts are expected near southeastern Louisiana. While no changes were made to the watches in the evening advisory, additional watches or warnings could be issued later tonight or Tuesday.
Bertha’s slow movement will prolong impacts across the northern Gulf Coast. Persistent onshore winds could produce up to 3 feet of storm surge from the Florida Panhandle through the central Gulf Coast, including Mobile Bay, while dangerous surf and rough marine conditions continue through midweek. Heavy rainfall will also become an increasing concern, with isolated totals exceeding 6 inches possible. The heaviest rain is expected to shift from the Florida Peninsula into the Florida Panhandle, coastal Alabama and Mississippi, and southern Louisiana as Bertha slowly tracks westward.
Rain chances are still possible on Tuesday across the western portion of the Peninsula, but much lower than previously anticipated as Bertha moves away and the wind shear is keeping its deepest storms closer to the Central Gulf.

Tropical Storm Bertha in the Gulf of Mexico is moving toward the Florida Panhandle and Alabama
sources.text:
Tropical Storm Bertha in the Gulf of Mexico is moving toward the Florida Panhandle and Alabama
Tropical Storm Bertha has strengthened in the Gulf of Mexico and is moving toward the Florida Panhandle and Alabama, causing a tropical storm warning and storm surge watches
NEW ORLEANS (AP) — Tropical Storm Bertha strengthened in the Gulf of Mexico and was moving slowly toward the Florida Panhandle and Alabama, causing a tropical storm warning and storm surge watches, forecasters said.
The storm was about 110 miles (177 kilometers) south of Panama City, Florida, and 170 miles (274 kilometers) southeast of Mobile, Alabama, and moving northwest at 5 mph (8 kph) with maximum sustained winds of 50 mph (80 kph), the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said Tuesday morning.
The wind speed increased by 10 mph (16 kph) since Bertha formed Monday night. A tropical storm warning, meaning the conditions are expected within the warning area within 36 hours, was in effect early Tuesday from the Florida and Alabama border to the Jefferson and Plaquemines parish line in Louisiana.
A storm surge watch, indicating rising, possible life-threatening water moving inland from the coast within 48 hours, was issued from the Alabama and Florida border to the mouth of the Mississippi River, the hurricane center reported.
Bertha is expected to stay near or along the Gulf Coast
The storm was expected to stay near or along the northern Gulf Coast this week, dropping heavy rain on coastal areas of Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana while pushing west toward Texas.
Potentially life-threatening storm surges of up to 4 feet (1.2 meters) are possible in portions of Louisiana, Alabama and Florida, the hurricane center said, warning Bertha could spin off an isolated tornado or two over the Florida Big Bend region.
Areas of flash flooding also will be possible through Friday along the coast from western Florida to middle Texas, forecasters said, adding that rainfall could total 3 to 5 inches (7 to 12 centimeters) along the Louisiana coastline, with higher amounts in some scattered areas.
Red flags on the beach at Orange Beach, Alabama, cautioned swimmers about high surf and currents. In Escambia County, Florida, emergency officials offered sand for people living in flood-prone areas to use for sandbags.
Hurricane Fausto churns in the Pacific
In the eastern Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Fausto churned far from Mexico’s Baja California peninsula and posed no threat to land, the hurricane center said.
Fausto gained hurricane status Monday night. It was about 740 miles (1,191 kilometers) southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula, had top sustained winds of 80 mph (129 kph) and was moving northwest at 12 mph (19 kph).
The storm was expected to strengthen Tuesday and Wednesday. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect, though ocean swells generated by the storm could cause life-threatening surf and rip tide conditions on the Baja California coast, the center said.

Tropical Storm Bertha Takes Aim at Gulf Coast as Texas Victims Begin Recovery from Recent Floods
Tropical Storm Bertha is strengthening as it heads for the U.S. Gulf Coast. It's expected to make landfall anywhere from Florida to Louisiana, with possible effects reaching as far west as Texas.
The National Hurricane Center reported on Tuesday morning that the storm was about 110 miles south of Panama City, Florida, and 170 miles southeast of Mobile, Alabama.
As of Tuesday morning, Bertha had maximum sustained winds of 50 mph, but the storm only formed on Monday night and is already picking up wind speed.
Heavy rain, coastal flooding, and tropical storm-force winds are all expected over the coming days. Potentially life-threatening storm surges of up to 4 feet are possible in portions of Louisiana, Alabama, and Florida, the hurricane center said.
Texas Already Dealing with Catastrophic Flooding
In Texas, where many communities are still recovering from last week’s catastrophic flooding, the long road to recovery is just beginning.
Operation Blessing is already on the ground in Kerrville, setting up a food truck to serve hot meals to families affected by the flooding.
OB relief teams are also partnering with a local church to distribute pallets of cleanup supplies and hygiene kits.
Many of these same hurting Texas Hill Country communities are still recovering from the devastating Fourth of July flooding in 2025, when catastrophic flash floods claimed more than 130 lives across Central Texas, including many in Kerr County and children from Camp Mystic.
During that response, Operation Blessing provided emergency meals, cleanup supplies, volunteer assistance, and encouragement to families as they began the difficult work of rebuilding.

sources.news_title: Tropical Storm Bertha tracker map shows where landfall expected this week
sources.text:
Tropical Storm Bertha is forecast to track near the northern Gulf Coast over the coming days, bringing heavy rainfall, coastal flooding and a potentially “life-threatening” storm surge to parts of Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC).
The storm strengthened Monday night after hurricane hunter aircraft data confirmed that Tropical Depression Two had officially become Tropical Storm Bertha, the second named storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.
As of the NHC's latest advisory early on Tuesday morning, Bertha was located in the northeastern Gulf, about 175 miles southeast of Mobile, Alabama. Maximum sustained winds have increased to 50 mph, while the storm was moving northwest at just 5 mph.
"A slow northwestward to west-northwestward motion is expected today followed by a turn toward the west by the middle part of this week," NHC said in the latest forecast.
Where Is Tropical Storm Bertha Headed?
Forecasters expect Bertha to remain close to the northern Gulf Coast as it gradually drifts westward.
On Tuesday, NHC extended the tropical storm warning from the Florida Panhandle to the Terrebonne/Lafourche Parish line in Louisiana.
"Bertha will move near or along the northern Gulf Coast during the next several days," the Miami-based NHC said.
The official NHC forecast track shows the center of the storm approaching southeastern Louisiana by late Wednesday before tracking westward along the northern Gulf Coast later in the week. While some fluctuations in the track remain possible, according to the NHC forecast at the time of publishing, the system is expected to approach the Louisiana-Mississippi coast as a tropical storm rather than a hurricane.
NHC Deputy Director Jamie Rhome said that a southerly wind is "impeding additional development," meaning that the storm may weaken.
"At this point, we believe that the northern vertical here that we just talked about, and land interaction from dry air, and that's a weakening trend," Rhome said, adding, "It looks like it's been convenient for all of the hazards displaced just offshore."
Storm Surge and Flooding Threat
A storm surge watch was replaced with a coastal flood warning Tuesday with minor to moderate coastal flooding still expected to occur between the Mississippi-Alabama border and the mouth of the Mississippi River.
NHC forecasts that the storm surge could raise water levels by 2 to 4 feet above normally dry ground from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Alabama-Florida border, if the surge coincides with high tide.
Heavy rainfall is also expected across the Gulf Coast through Friday. The NHC's rainfall outlook projects widespread totals of 2 to 4 inches from western Florida to Texas, with isolated amounts reaching 8 inches.
Forecasters warn that flash flooding is possible, particularly in urban and low-lying areas.
Tornado Risk and Wind Impacts
In addition to flooding, forecasters from The Weather Channel say Bertha could produce isolated tornadoes and tropical-storm-force winds, which are expected to sweep along portions of the northern Gulf Coast through Wednesday.
The NHC has issued tropical storm warnings from the Alabama-Florida border westward to the Jefferson/Plaquemines Parish border in Louisiana. Tropical storm watches remain posted for parts of the Florida Panhandle, metropolitan New Orleans and additional sections of the Louisiana coast.
What Experts Are Saying
Alex DaSilva, AccuWeather's lead hurricane expert, said environmental conditions are expected to limit major strengthening, according to The South Florida Reporter.
"Dry air and hostile wind shear across the Gulf will be the biggest factors in whether this depression organizes," DaSilva said. "Right now, our forecast expects those conditions to prevent significant strengthening...the next 24 to 48 hours will be key as to where this storm will move later in the week."
Dr. Ryan Truchelut of WeatherTiger described Bertha primarily as a rainfall threat rather than a significant wind event.
"Under any realistic scenario, [Tropical Storm Bertha] is predominantly a rainmaker," Truchelut said, adding that he expects “Periodic rainbands” to spread across inland North Florida over the next two days, expanding into the western Panhandle and eastern Louisiana on Tuesday and Wednesday. “In general, expect rain totals of 2-4 inches along the immediate coast from Cedar Key to Mobile, as well as in Southeast Louisiana; look for another 1-2 inches for inland North Florida through the end of the week.”
Residents across the northern Gulf Coast are being urged to monitor forecasts from the NHC and local National Weather Service offices as Bertha moves closer to land and warnings may be expanded or updated over the next 24 to 48 hours.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Robinson, Cristina Diciu, Tony Phillips, Sam Wilson.

sources.news_title: Tropical Storm Bertha in the Gulf moving toward Florida Panhandle and Alabama
sources.text:
NEW ORLEANS – Tropical Storm Bertha strengthened in the Gulf of Mexico on Tuesday but was expected to weaken as it chugs closer to the U.S., potentially bringing coastal flooding and heavy rain from the Florida Panhandle to Louisiana.
Those areas along the northern Gulf Coast were under a tropical storm warning through Wednesday and could see rain and flooding into Thursday morning, the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said. New Orleans also was under a tropical storm warning.
Recommended Videos
The storm was about 105 miles (170 kilometers) southwest of Panama City, Florida, and roughly the same distance southeast of Mobile, Alabama. It was moving slowly to the northwest Tuesday afternoon with maximum sustained winds of 60 mph (95 kph), the hurricane center said Tuesday. Gradual weakening was forecast through Friday.
Bertha was forecast to make landfall Wednesday night somewhere in the coastal and lightly populated part of Louisiana southeast of New Orleans, said Michael Buchanan, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Louisiana.
Wind will be biggest threat there, he said.
Authorities open sites to distribute sandbags
Authorities in Mississippi, Louisiana and Florida opened sites to provide sandbags to residents while red flag warnings were posted along some beaches advising swimmers about the dangers of rip tides.
Up and down the coast, double red flags signaled that Gulf waters were closed for swimming.
Beaches near Pensacola, Florida, were mostly deserted except for tourists venturing out to take photos of the pounding surf.
“For locals, this is just another storm,” said Candice Henderson, manager of the Crab Trap, a beachside restaurant that was packed Tuesday on Pensacola’s Perdido Key. “When you’re on vacation and its raining, you either shop or you go out to eat.”
The storm was expected to weaken as it moves along the coast, said Jamie Rhome of the hurricane center. It's possible that the worst of the storm will stay offshore, he said Tuesday.
Bertha was expected to weaken further as it pushes into Texas, forecasters said.
Forecasts called for as much as 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 centimeters) of rain from western Florida to the southern Louisiana coastline, with higher amounts in some scattered areas.
That could cause flash flooding in some urban areas.
Authorities also advised that areas in Louisiana from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Alabama-Mississippi state line could see storm surges of up to 4 feet (1.2 meters). Parts of Florida and Alabama could see smaller surges.
The tropical storm warning extended west to Morgan City, Louisiana.
Bertha is the second tropical storm of the Atlantic hurricane season
Bertha is the second tropical storm of the Atlantic hurricane season. Tropical Storm Arthur last month brought heavy rainfall to the southeastern U.S.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration expects this year to see a below-average Atlantic hurricane season although that doesn’t eliminate the chances of a catastrophic storm.
Bertha could dump heavy rain on coastal areas of Mississippi that are still recovering from flooding brought by Arthur that destroyed and damaged homes in June.
“Because of that, people are definitely paying attention, or at least you would hope so,” said Jeff Clark, a spokesperson for Mississippi's Harrison County, where six sites were open for sandbag distribution.
So far, there hasn't been a need to open any shelters or order evacuations, Clark said on Tuesday.
Hurricane Fausto churns in the Pacific
In the eastern Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Fausto churned far from Mexico’s Baja California peninsula and posed no threat to land, the hurricane center said.
Fausto gained hurricane status Monday night. It was about 780 miles (1,260 kilometers) southwest of the southern tip of Baja California, had top sustained winds of 75 mph (120 kph) and was moving west-northwest at 12 mph (19 kph).
The storm was expected to strengthen Tuesday and Wednesday. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect, though ocean swells generated by the storm could cause life-threatening surf and rip tide conditions on the Baja California coast, the center said.

sources.news_title: Tropical Storm Bertha slowly strengthens, threatening flooding as it trudges toward Gulf Coast
sources.text:
Tropical Storm Bertha has strengthened in the northeastern Gulf, where it is expected to bring periods of rain, gusty winds and coastal flooding to parts of the Gulf Coast from Florida to Louisiana.
🌀 ⛈️ Get your storm forecast in the CNN Weather app
Bertha’s maximum sustained winds increased from 50 mph to 60 mph late Tuesday morning, but the storm is expected to have little change in strength for the rest of Tuesday.
Bertha may have intensified, but it still isn’t a well-organized tropical storm. Most of its thunderstorms remain confined to its southern half because unfavorable upper-level winds and dry air continue to disrupt development despite fuel from near-record warm Gulf water.
This lopsided structure will keep much of Bertha’s heaviest rain and strongest winds offshore as it crawls westward along the northern Gulf Coast through Wednesday.
Still, tropical storm conditions are beginning to spread into the immediate coast of the Florida Panhandle Tuesday afternoon, the National Hurricane Center said. The storm is also hurling bands of rain and rough surf into parts of the northern Gulf Coast.
Bertha’s moisture will also help fuel a flooding rain threat hundreds of miles away in the Southeast. A stalling cold front in the region will pull its moisture up from the Gulf Wednesday through the end of the week, especially over the Carolinas and southeast Virginia.
Bertha is the second named storm of the Atlantic hurricane season, which has gotten off to a slow start compared to recent years as El Niño tightens its grip on parts of the basin.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration predicts a lower-than-average number of named systems in the Atlantic this season because of it.
Storm track, intensity
Bertha will most likely track along the Gulf Coast and make landfall or graze the coast of southeast Louisiana by early Wednesday evening as a weak tropical storm.
Bertha is then forecast to track toward the Upper Texas Coast while weakening to a tropical depression later this week, but it might not make it that far west. The storm-killing wind shear Bertha is battling now could cause it to dissipate sooner near the Louisiana coast.
Wind shear is the change in speed or direction of winds in the upper levels of the atmosphere that literally shears, or rips, storms apart. It’s also the reason most of Bertha’s thunderstorms are south of its center.
Land interaction with the Gulf Coast will eventually pile onto the hostile conditions by depriving Bertha of the warm, moist ocean conditions that are fueling its thunderstorms.
Impacts expected on Gulf Coast
Regardless of the system’s fate, bands of rain, gusty winds and some coastal flooding will impact the northern Gulf Coast through at least Thursday.
A tropical storm warning has been issued for the western Florida Panhandle, coastal Alabama, Mississippi and far southeastern Louisiana. In these areas, tropical storm conditions — sustained 39+ mph winds — are expected within the next 36 hours. Tropical storm watches are in effect as far west as south-central Louisiana.
Here’s what to expect:
• Rainfall: Totals of 1 to 4 inches, with up to 6 inches in the strongest thunderstorms, are possible from the western Florida Panhandle to southern portions of Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana and possibly the Texas coast. This could trigger localized flash flooding, especially in urban areas like New Orleans.
• Wind: Sustained winds of 39+ mph are expected in the tropical storm warning area of the western Florida Panhandle, Alabama, Mississippi and southeastern Louisiana coasts late Tuesday into Wednesday. Higher gusts in thunderstorms could cause isolated power outages.
• Storm surge: Water levels could rise 2 to 4 feet above normal from the mouth of the Mississippi River in southeast Louisiana to the Alabama-Florida border, especially with the Wednesday and Thursday morning high tides. A coastal flood warning is in effect for the southeast Louisiana and Mississippi coasts, where moderate coastal flooding is possible in low-lying areas.
• Dangerous beach conditions: Rough surf and a high risk of rip currents will continue to impact beaches from the Florida Panhandle westward to Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana through at least Thursday. These are life-threatening conditions for even the strongest swimmers.

sources.text:
Tropical Storm Bertha drifts toward land; Hurricane Fausto forms in Pacific
NEW ORLEANS (AP) — Tropical Storm Bertha formed Monday evening in the Gulf of Mexico south of the Florida Panhandle as it drifts erratically toward populated coastal areas bearing a threat of heavy rain, storm surge and damaging wind gusts, forecasters say.
Meanwhile, in the eastern Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Fausto formed far from Mexico’s Baja California peninsula and posed no threat to land Monday night.
The center of Bertha was located about 140 miles (225 km) south of Panama City, Florida, in the northern Gulf. Maximum sustained winds were around 40 mph (65 kph) and some additional strengthening is expected as the storm approaches land, according to the Miami-based National Hurricane Center.
The slow-moving storm drifted for hours on Monday, but is expected to stay near or along the northern Gulf Coast early this week, unleashing heavy rain on coastal areas of Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana as it pushes west toward Texas.
Bertha is the second tropical storm of the Atlantic hurricane season. Tropical Storm Arthur last month brought heavy rainfall to the southeastern United States.
The storm was nearly stationary by Monday night, but it was expected to make a west-northwestward or westward turn toward the coast over the next few days, according to the hurricane center.
A tropical storm warning is in effect for a wide area from the Alabama-Florida border westward to southeastern Louisiana at the Jefferson and Plaquemines parish line. A storm surge watch also has been posted from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Alabama-Florida border on the Gulf Coast.
Potentially life-threatening storm surges of up to four feet (1.2 meters) could occur in portions of the Louisiana, Alabama and Florida, the hurricane center said, warning Bertha could spin off an isolated tornado or two over the Florida Big Bend region in the week.
Areas of flash flooding will also be possible through Friday along the coast from western Florida to middle Texas, forecasters said. They added that rainfall could total 3 to 5 inches (7 to 12 centimeters) along the Louisiana coastline with higher amounts in some scattered areas.
Red flags were flying on the beach at Orange Beach, Alabama, cautioning swimmers about high surf and currents. In Escambia County, Florida, emergency officials offered sand for people living in flood-prone areas to use for sandbags.
Fausto gained hurricane status Monday night and was about 745 miles (1,200 km) southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula, forecasters said.
The U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said Fausto had top sustained winds of 75 mph (120 kph) and was moving to the west-northwest at 9 mph 15 (kph).
No coastal watches or warnings were in effect though ocean swells generated by the storm could pummel the Baja California coast and cause life-threatening surf and rip tide conditions, the center said.

Tropical Storm Bertha has formed in the Gulf of Mexico and is moving northwest toward the southeastern United States, according to the report.
The National Hurricane Center said the system strengthened into a tropical storm after NOAA Hurricane Hunters confirmed maximum sustained winds of 40 mph.
The report said Bertha is expected to bring widespread rainfall of up to six inches, with isolated areas receiving as much as eight inches through Friday, increasing the risk of flash flooding along parts of the Gulf Coast.
According to the report, Bertha is not expected to cross into the Atlantic Ocean, but moisture from the storm could interact with a weather front near North Carolina's Outer Banks later this week, potentially producing additional heavy rainfall across the Carolinas.

Tropical Storm Bertha forms in the Gulf, forecasts warn of flooding
Editor's note: Follow the latest updates about Tropical Storm Bertha in USA TODAY's coverage for Tuesday, July 21.
Tropical Storm Bertha was "stationary" on the night of July 20 as federal forecasters warned it could bring tropical storm conditions, heavy rainfall and coastal flooding to parts of the northern Gulf Coast in the coming days.
Bertha, the second named storm of the Atlantic hurricane season, intensified from a tropical depression on July 20, according to the National Hurricane Center.
The storm was located about 140 miles south of Panama City, Florida, and about 215 miles southeast of Mobile, Alabama, as of the hurricane center's 10 p.m. CDT advisory. Bertha had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph.
Forecasters said a slow west-northwestward or westward movement is expected during the next several days, with Bertha forecast to move near or along the northern Gulf Coast. Some additional strengthening is possible through July 21.
Tropical storm watches were in effect along the Gulf Coast, where strong winds, heavy rain and dangerous surf conditions could develop late July 20 into July 21, according to the hurricane center. A storm surge watch was in effect from the Alabama-Florida border to the mouth of the Mississippi River.
Forecasters advised authorities and residents in Louisiana and Texas to monitor the progress of the storm, as "additional watches or warnings could be required for portions of that area" on July 21.
Flooding possible
The hurricane center said that Bertha is "expected to produce rainfall amounts of 2 to 4 inches with locally higher totals around 8 inches through Friday along the Gulf Coast and adjacent inland locations from western Florida to the Middle Texas Coast, including southern portions of Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana. This rainfall may produce areas of flash flooding, especially in urban areas."
In an online update, AccuWeather meteorologist Alex DaSilva said that "while rainfall will be welcome across portions of the Florida Panhandle due to an ongoing drought, the flooding risk can be increased due to dry soil. This dry, hard soil can allow the water to run off instead of being absorbed right away."
If heavy rain shifts farther west into the Texas Hill Country, there will be elevated concern for flash flooding given the terrain and recent significant flooding that occurred across the region, AccuWeather warned.
Second storm of what's expected to be a quiet year
The storm comes about a month after Tropical Storm Arthur formed in the Gulf.
Forecasters predict the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season will see "below-normal" activity levels, thanks largely to the storm-snuffing impacts of El Niño.
A total of eight to 14 named storms are expected, with anywhere from three to six becoming hurricanes, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's seasonal outlook predicts.
A typical year averages about 14 tropical storms, seven of which spin into hurricanes, based on weather records from 1991 to 2020.

Tropical Storm Bertha strengthens, threatening Gulf Coast
sources.text:
Tropical Storm Bertha strengthens, threatening Gulf Coast. See forecast map and its path.
Tropical Storm Bertha was threatening the Gulf Coast on Tuesday with heavy rain as its projected path sparked watches and warnings along the coastal region.
Bertha is in the northeastern Gulf of Mexico with maximum sustained winds of 60 mph, up from 50 mph earlier in the day, according to the National Hurricane Center, which said tropical storm conditions were beginning to spread over portions of the Florida Panhandle on Tuesday afternoon. The storm is expected to impact the coasts of western Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana through Thursday.
Map shows projected path
Bertha's strength isn't expected to change much on Tuesday, and the system — which is the second named storm of the Atlantic hurricane season — is forecast to gradually weaken as the week progresses. As of Tuesday evening, it was moving northwest at about 6 mph.
The storm is expected to turn west-northwest Tuesday night, the hurricane center said. The storm is expected to continue with "westward motion forecast Wednesday through Friday. On the forecast track, Bertha will move near or along the northern Gulf Coast during the next couple of days or so."
Warnings and watches in effect
A tropical storm warning was in effect Tuesday from the Bay/Gulf County line in Florida to Morgan City, Louisiana, as well as for New Orleans and Lake Pontchartrain.
A tropical storm watch was posted for west of Morgan City to Cameron, Louisiana, and Lake Maurepas.
A storm surge watch that was in effect earlier for the northern Gulf Coast has been discontinued.
"Tropical storm conditions are expected within the warning area along the northern Gulf coast by late today into Wednesday," the hurricane center said. "Tropical storm conditions are possible within the watch area in Louisiana by Wednesday."
Forecasters warned of rainfall up to 6 inches in some areas. Rain was expected through Thursday along the central Gulf Coast, stretching from western Florida to southern Louisiana, and forecasters warned of possible flash flooding.
The system could also produce storm surge, raising waters up to 4 feet in some locations along the coast.
Bertha comes weeks after the 2026 hurricane season's first named storm, Tropical Storm Arthur, which made landfall in June along the Gulf Coast of Texas.

sources.news_title: Tropical Storm Bertha forms in the Gulf of Mexico and could bring heavy rain to US coastal areas, forecasters say
Tropical Storm Bertha Expected to Form as Depression Nears Gulf Coast
sources.text:
A second named storm of the 2026 hurricane season has formed off the coast of Florida Monday evening.
Tropical Storm Bertha has strengthened from a tropical depression into a storm, the National Hurricane Center said in a 7 p.m. CT update.
While it has been “drifting erratically,” traveling around 3 mph, it is expected to move northwest tonight into Tuesday morning, “followed by a west-northwestward or westward motion.”
Positioned 110 miles south of Panama City, Florida, and 190 miles southeast of Mobile, Alabama, Bertha is expected to inch its way off the coast of Florida’s Big Bend to then scrape across the rest of the Gulf Coast states over the next several days.
Its maximum sustained winds increased from 35 mph to 40 mph since the previous 4 p.m. CT advisory. Sustained winds of at least 39 mph mark the threshold of a tropical depression becoming a tropical storm.
Tropical Storm watches are in effect for the entire stretch of Gulf Coast between Ochlockonee River, Florida, to the Jefferson/Plaquemines Parish border in Louisiana.
A storm surge warning is in effect for the Florida–Alabama state line and the mouth of the Mississippi River.
The National Hurricane Center is predicting as much as two to four feet of surge for those areas, with other areas from Indian Pass, Florida, to Chassahowitzka, Florida, and from Morgan City, Louisiana, to the mouth of the Mississippi River receiving one to three feet.
Lake Ponchartrain is also expected to receive one to three feet of storm surge.
The National Hurricane Center said that surf-related flooding will be dependent upon the time of the surge relative to the tide cycle.
In terms of rainfall, two to four inches is forecast across the Gulf Coast, with isolated areas expected to get as much as eight inches. Flash flooding could be possible in urban areas.
This storm spent several days off the west coast of Florida’s peninsula generating the counterclockwise rotation identified with tropical storms and hurricanes.
It threw bands of wind and rain and rip currents over Tampa Bay and most of Florida’s west coast across the Big Bend and Nature Coast through Panama City.
Those bands brought several inches of rain and wind gusts exceeding 45 mph.
The focal point of this storm’s development has continued to move west from the Florida–Georgia line, over the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf of America.
Tropical Storm Bertha comes a little more than one month after Tropical Storm Arthur, which briefly affected Galveston, Texas, the surrounding northeast corner of the Lone Star State’s Gulf Coast, and parts of western Louisiana.

sources.news_title: Gulf depression forecast to become tropical storm
sources.text:
US News
Gulf depression forecast to become tropical storm
Tropical Depression Two remains below tropical storm strength in the eastern Gulf, but it is forecast to strengthen on Tuesday as it moves slowly toward the northern Gulf Coast.
The depression has maximum sustained winds of about 35 miles per hour as of 4 p.m. CDT Monday, unchanged from the morning. It is moving slowly toward the northwest at about 3 miles per hour.
The National Hurricane Center (NHC) said the depression became better organized during the day, with a more defined circulation and increased thunderstorms near its center. Data from an Air Force Reserve Hurricane Hunter aircraft, however, showed that its winds remain below tropical storm strength.
The system is forecast to move slowly toward the northwest or west-northwest through early Wednesday before turning west. Its center is expected to move near or along the northern Gulf Coast, but forecast models disagree on how close it will come to land.
Some models take the depression inland along the northern Gulf Coast, while others keep its center farther offshore.
The depression is expected to become a tropical storm as bursts of thunderstorms develop near and south of its center. Forecasters predict peak winds of about 50 miles per hour within 36 hours.
Strong northeasterly wind shear is then expected to disrupt the system, ending further strengthening and causing it to weaken. The depression could become a remnant low within five days or dissipate sooner because of wind shear and interaction with land.
The wind shear is also expected to give the system an uneven structure, with most of its rain and wind occurring south of the center. Outer bands could bring tropical storm conditions to parts of the Florida Panhandle beginning Monday night.

sources.news_title: ‘Worth keeping tabs on’: Tropical Storm Bertha in northeastern Gulf could impact Texas
sources.text:
Tropical Storm Bertha in the northeastern Gulf is expected to gradually strengthen as it moves west, according to the National Hurricane Center, which says the system has the potential to bring flash flooding and strong winds to Texas later this week.
At 7 p.m. Monday, the National Hurricane Center officially upgraded the storm from a tropical disturbance to Tropical Storm Bertha. It is the second tropical storm this hurricane season after Tropical Storm Arthur formed in the western Gulf in mid-June and brought heavy rain and strong winds to coastal areas including Galveston.
Cameron Self, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service’s Houston/Galveston office, said Monday that weather-monitoring planes from the U.S. Air Force and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) began flying into the system Sunday evening and will continue to monitor it as it makes its way through the Gulf.
"Even though right now the forecast is not showing significant impacts to our area, any storm in the Gulf is worth keeping tabs on," Self told Houston Public Media on Monday morning. "So we'd recommend checking on the [depression] at least once a day just in case."
The system could bring tropical storm conditions to parts of the Gulf Coast, from the Florida panhandle to southeastern Louisiana, by Monday night or early Tuesday, according to a 10 a.m. advisory from the National Hurricane Center.
Bertha is not expected to have a major impact on the Texas coast, according to Monday forecasts from the National Weather Service, which said its forecast was "highly uncertain" beyond Thursday. Projections as of Monday morning show the majority of Southeast Texas, south Louisiana and Mississippi in the potential path of the system.
Self said the forecast will solidify throughout the week.
"Currently it is still in the northeast Gulf, and it's moving very slowly to the northwest," Self said. "We do expect it to turn more toward the west in the general direction of Texas, but the system does have some hurdles it's going to have to get through before it's able to get here."
One of the potential hurdles is if the system makes landfall in Louisiana, Self said.
"If that's the case, that'll take the system from being over the Gulf to over land, which would certainly limit the amount that it could intensify, if not weaken it," he said. "Also there's a lot of shear and dry air that it's dealing with."
However, the system is still expected to strengthen before the end of the week, Self said.
"The conditions are not necessarily so unfavorable to where the system can't strengthen,” he said. “It likely is going to strengthen some ... but right now as it stands, it's not looking like a major impact to Southeast Texas."
Editor’s note: This article was updated on July 20.

sources.news_title: It's official! Tropical Storm Bertha on the Gulf; tropical storm and storm surge watches in effect for parts of Florida
sources.text:
The National Hurricane Center has upgraded Tropical Depression Two to Tropical Storm Bertha after NOAA Hurricane Hunters found the system had strengthened during Monday afternoon. Bertha now has maximum sustained winds of 40 mph, is moving west-northwest at 5 mph, and has a minimum central pressure of 1004 mb.
Tropical Storm #Bertha has formed in the northeastern Gulf - the 2nd named storm of the 2026 Atlantic #hurricane season. On average, the 2nd Atlantic named storm forms on 17 July. pic.twitter.com/Lxj7uCAmN9
— Philip Klotzbach (@philklotzbach) July 20, 2026
Although Bertha has strengthened into a tropical storm, its overall organization remains limited. Dry air wrapping into the circulation and strong wind shear of around 25 knots (and increasing over its east and northeast) are expected to prevent rapid intensification as the storm drifts slowly across the northeastern Gulf of Mexico. Hurricane Hunters also observed the center wobbling throughout the day as the storm remains trapped between two areas of high pressure, resulting in weak steering currents and an erratic motion. Additional reconnaissance flights are scheduled through Wednesday, and slight adjustments to the forecast track remain possible.
Bertha is expected to continue moving very slowly through Tuesday before gradually turning more westward later this week. The National Hurricane Center continues to forecast a track toward southeastern Louisiana on Wednesday, although the cone of uncertainty still allows for the center to remain offshore. If Bertha spends more time over the warm Gulf waters, some additional strengthening is possible despite the unfavorable environment.
Tropical Storm Watch and Storm Surge Watch in effect for parts of the Panhandle.
Tropical Storm Watches remain in effect from the Florida Panhandle westward to Plaquemines Parish, Louisiana, with a Storm Surge Watch extending from the Alabama-Florida border to the mouth of the Mississippi River. Tropical-storm-force winds are expected to begin affecting the western Florida Panhandle Monday night, especially from Panama City Beach to Pensacola, before spreading along the Mississippi and Alabama coasts on Tuesday. By Tuesday night, stronger wind gusts are expected near southeastern Louisiana. While no changes were made to the watches in the evening advisory, additional watches or warnings could be issued later tonight or Tuesday.
Bertha's slow movement will prolong impacts across the northern Gulf Coast. Persistent onshore winds could produce up to 3 feet of storm surge from the Florida Panhandle through the central Gulf Coast, including Mobile Bay, while dangerous surf and rough marine conditions continue through midweek. Heavy rainfall will also become an increasing concern, with isolated totals exceeding 6 inches possible. The heaviest rain is expected to shift from the Florida Peninsula into the Florida Panhandle, coastal Alabama and Mississippi, and southern Louisiana as Bertha slowly tracks westward.
Rain chances are still possible on Tuesday across the western portion of the Peninsula, but much lower than previously anticipated as Bertha moves away and the wind shear is keeping its deepest storms closer to the Central Gulf.

Tropical Storm Bertha has formed in the Gulf of Mexico, prompting storm surge and tropical storm watches along the northern Gulf Coast as the system moves slowly toward the west-northwest.
Data from NOAA Hurricane Hunter aircraft confirmed Monday evening that a tropical depression off the Florida Panhandle had strengthened into the second named storm of the Atlantic hurricane season. A tropical storm watch was in place from Florida’s western border to Mississippi on Monday due to a depression expected to become a named storm later in the day.

sources.news_title: Louisiana residents should review insurance before Bertha arrives
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – Louisiana Insurance Commissioner Tim Temple is urging residents to review their insurance coverage and prepare their homes as Tropical Depression Two, which is expected to strengthen into Tropical Storm Bertha, moves toward the northern Gulf Coast.
Forecasters expect the system to gradually organize before tracking westward along the Gulf Coast, bringing the potential for heavy rain, gusty winds and coastal flooding to southeastern Louisiana beginning Wednesday. While the storm is not expected to significantly affect the state through Tuesday, the National Weather Service says the greatest impacts are expected Wednesday into early Thursday.
"Regardless of how this storm develops, Louisianans should continue to monitor the weather and take steps to be insurance ready," Temple said Monday.
He urged residents to trim trees, clear gutters and storm drains, secure outdoor furniture and review emergency plans before conditions deteriorate.
The Louisiana Department of Insurance also recommends reviewing homeowners and flood insurance policies before the storm arrives, particularly deductible amounts. Named storm or hurricane deductibles typically range from 2% to 5% of a home's insured value. For example, a homeowner with a $200,000 insured home and a 3% hurricane deductible would pay the first $6,000 of covered damage before insurance benefits begin.
The National Weather Service has issued Tropical Storm and Storm Surge watches for portions of Louisiana's immediate coast east of the mouth of the Mississippi River, including eastern Orleans Parish. Forecasters caution that watches could be expanded as the forecast evolves.
Forecasts call for sustained winds near 50 mph at peak intensity, with tropical-storm-force wind probabilities of 40% to 50% across southern Plaquemines Parish and lower chances elsewhere in southeast Louisiana. Gusts could down tree limbs, damage awnings and produce isolated power outages.
Storm surge remains one of the primary concerns along the coast. The National Weather Service forecasts 2 to 4 feet of inundation above ground level east of the Mississippi River and 1 to 3 feet elsewhere along the Louisiana coast, potentially flooding low-lying roads, damaging marinas and causing moderate beach erosion.
Rainfall forecasts remain highly dependent on the storm's eventual track. Most areas north of the Interstate 10/12 corridor are expected to receive less than an inch of rain, while Louisiana's immediate southeast coast could receive 2 to 5 inches, with isolated flooding possible where heavier rain bands develop. Forecasters noted the storm is expected to be lopsided, with most of its rain and strongest winds remaining south of the center over the Gulf.
The weather service also warned residents not to overlook another hazard: extreme heat. Heat index values between 107 and 111 degrees are expected Monday and Tuesday, and dangerous heat could continue into midweek if cloud cover and rainfall remain limited north of the storm's center.
Insurance officials recommend documenting homes and belongings with photos or video before the storm arrives, keeping insurance policies and agent contact information readily available in case evacuation becomes necessary and saving receipts for temporary repairs should damage occur.
If damage occurs, residents should contact their insurance company immediately, photograph property before cleanup begins and take reasonable steps to prevent additional damage, such as covering damaged roofs with tarps or boarding broken windows.
The National Weather Service said confidence is moderate that southeastern Louisiana will experience tropical-storm-force wind gusts, minor to moderate coastal flooding, isolated flooding from heavy rainfall and dangerous marine conditions during the middle of the week, while the tornado threat currently remains low.

sources.text:
Tropical Storm Bertha is gaining strength in the north Gulf and is expected to hit portions of the Gulf Coast from Florida to Louisiana, and possibly as far west as Texas.
Heavy rain, coastal flooding and tropical storm-force winds are all possible through the week in its path.
The second named storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season had winds of 60 mph as of Tuesday afternoon and additional strengthening is possible. Forecasters said the tropical storm had become better organized over the previous 24 hours.
A Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for areas of the Gulf Coast from the Alabama/Florida border to the Jefferson/Plaquemines Parish border in Louisiana.
A tropical storm watch has been issued for the coast of the Bay/Gulf County line in Florida westward to the Florida/Alabama border, west of the Jefferson/Plaquemines Parish border to Morgan City, Louisiana, and metropolitan New Orleans. In these locations, tropical storm conditions are possible within the next 24 to 48 hours. Additional watches could be issued farther west along the Louisiana and Texas coast in the next day or two.
IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Tropical Storm Arthur, first of 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, makes landfall
Atlantic hurricane season has gotten off to a slow start compared to recent years as El Niño tightens its grip on parts of the basin.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration predicts a lower-than-average number of named systems in the Atlantic this season because of it.
Storm track, intensity
Bertha will most likely track along or make landfall on the northern Gulf Coast near southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi by Wednesday.
This would prevent it from intensifying much because tropical systems weaken over land. It would also face an increasing amount of storm-killing wind shear, which is the change in speed or direction of winds in the upper levels of the atmosphere.
Those unfavorable factors could even cause the system to dissipate over Louisiana, but the latest forecast calls for it to reach the Upper Texas Coast as a tropical depression by late week.
Impacts expected on Gulf Coast
Regardless of the system’s fate, heavy rainfall, gusty winds and some coastal flooding will impact the northern Gulf Coast through at least midweek.
Here’s what to expect:
• Rainfall: Widespread totals of 2 to 4 inches, with up to 8 inches in the strongest thunderstorms, are possible from the western Florida Panhandle to southern portions of Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana and possibly the Texas coast. This could trigger flash flooding, especially in urban areas like New Orleans.
• Wind: Tropical storm conditions — sustained winds of 39+ mph— are possible in the tropical storm watch area of the Florida Panhandle Monday night into Tuesday. Locations farther west in a tropical storm watch could see those conditions late Tuesday night into Wednesday. Higher gusts in thunderstorms could cause isolated power outages.
• Storm surge: Water levels could rise 2 to 4 feet above normal from the mouth of the Mississippi River in southeast Louisiana to the Alabama-Florida border. A storm surge watch is in effect for this area, which means life-threatening inundation of ocean water is possible in the next 48 hours.

It is likely that there will be convective bursts near and south of the center during this time, and these should help intensify the cyclone to a tropical storm. After that, the northeasterly shear should increase, and the global models suggest it will get strong enough to destroy the vertical integrity of the cyclone. This should halt intensification and then cause weakening. The new intensity forecast calls for a peak intensity of 45 kt in 36 h, and this is at the upper edge of the intensity guidance. The new forecast also calls for the system to weaken to a remnant low by 120 h, and based on the dynamical model guidance, there is a possibility it could dissipate between 72 and 120 h due to shear and land interaction."
