Update (Monday, July 20, 8:30 p.m. EDT):
The National Hurricane Center has officially upgraded Tropical Depression Two to Tropical Storm Bertha in the 8:00 PM EDT advisory. NOAA Hurricane Hunters flew into the system throughout the afternoon and found that the depression had strengthened into a tropical storm. It currently has maximum sustained winds of 40 mph as it continues to crawl west-northwest at around 5 mph (6 km/h). The minimum central pressure has also dropped to 1004 millibars (29.65 inches of mercury). This is slightly lower than Bertha’s central pressure during Monday afternoon.
[Haz clic aquí para leer en español]
Bertha arrived just three days after the average date of the Atlantic’s second named storm of the season (July 17), based on the period 1991-2020. In contrast, the Eastern Pacific produced its sixth named storm of 2026, Fausto, on Sunday, July 19, more than two weeks earlier than average.
Tropical-storm-force winds could begin impacting the western portion of the Florida Panhandle coast Monday evening into Tuesday morning. Expect tropical-storm-force winds to mainly impact the immediate coastline from Panama City Beach to Pensacola.
Remember that the system will be moving very slowly. Therefore, tropical-storm-force winds will gradually increase throughout the day Tuesday along the Mississippi and Alabama coasts. Then, by Tuesday night, wind gusts will increase as the system moves closer to the southeastern portion of Louisiana, specifically Plaquemines Parish.
There are no changes in the Tropical Storm Watches currently in effect as of the early evening advisory. However, additional watches and warnings may be required later tonight or on Tuesday.
During this afternoon, Hurricane Hunters noticed that the center had been moving erratically for most of the day due to its position between the mid-level ridges. Hurricane Hunters are scheduled to fly the system again overnight, with three additional reconnaissance missions scheduled between Tuesday and Wednesday. Keep in mind that because the center is moving erratically, there could be slight shifts in the forecast track. Also, very strong wind shear is impacting and will continue to impact Bertha, limiting further intensification quickly, and keeping the most intense rainfall to the south of the storm for now. We will continue to monitor the system closely.
Original article, posted on Monday, July 20:
After what seemed like rapid development from Tropical Depression Two, the system has slowed in organization over the last 24 hours. Much of its lack of organization is due to dry air intruding into the system from the northeast, which prevented it from becoming better organized overnight Sunday. Wind shear also appears to be increasing and is expected to remain strong, around 25 knots, through Tuesday, which will keep this system from intensifying quickly while it crawls over the northeastern Gulf.
Weather pattern keeping TD 2 crawling
The high-pressure system centered over the central United States will continue to steer the storm, which will get the name Bertha if it intensifies to tropical storm status, primarily westward this week. Another area of high pressure over the western Atlantic is preventing the tropical system from being pulled northward by the trough currently digging across the eastern United States. As these two high-pressure systems sandwich the tropical depression, the storm has very little steering flow. Over the weekend, TD 2 became nearly stationary, and as of Monday morning, it was moving northwest at only about 3 mph (6 km/h). This slow movement is expected to continue through at least late Tuesday afternoon. Once TD 2 begins to accelerate, we expect it to make a more pronounced westward turn.
The National Hurricane Center‘s cone of uncertainty remains quite broad, with the forecast center ranging from a landfall near the southeastern Louisiana coast on Wednesday afternoon to a track that keeps it about 100 miles south of the coastline. If the center takes the southern track and remains over water, it could mean a bit more strengthening as waters are plenty warm between 85 and 87 degrees F (29 to 30 degrees C).
This will be an all-week system
The latest official forecast from the National Hurricane Center brings future Tropical Storm Bertha ashore over the marshes of eastern Plaquemines Parish before it slowly tracks across coastal Louisiana on Wednesday and Thursday. The system could then re-emerge over the far northwestern Gulf of Mexico, where it may make a second landfall as a tropical depression somewhere along the southeast Texas coast by late this week or early next weekend.
Tropical Storm Watches remain in effect from the Florida Panhandle westward to Plaquemines Parish in Louisiana. These will likely be upgraded to Tropical Storm Warnings later today or on Tuesday. There is also a Storm Surge Watch in effect from the Alabama/Florida Border to the Mouth of the Mississippi River, Louisiana. Winds are expected to begin increasing Monday night and continue through Tuesday across the watch area. Keep in mind that TD 2 will likely expand its wind field as it moves slowly. Storms that struggle with dry-air intrusion often compensate by becoming larger. Also remember that although moving slowly, the system will continue to gain latitude over the next day or two. As a result, persistent onshore winds will continue to produce hazardous surf and rough marine conditions along Florida’s west coast through the middle of the week.
The system’s west-northwest motion will also keep onshore winds blowing from the Florida Panhandle through the central Gulf Coast for much of the week. As a result, storm surge combined with several cycles of high tide will likely produce coastal flooding as water is pushed inland. Areas from the Florida Panhandle through the central Gulf Coast, including Mobile Bay, could experience up to 3 feet of storm surge.
The storm’s slow movement will also lead to prolonged periods of heavy rainfall across the Gulf Coast states. Rainfall totals could easily exceed 6 inches in isolated locations throughout the week.
TD 2 will bring drought-easing rains to Louisiana and the Florida Panhandle
The National Hurricane Center is forecasting the second tropical system of the season to bring rains of 6 inches for portions of southern Louisiana and the Florida Panhandle. While rains of this magnitude could well cause damaging flooding, they will also be beneficial: the Gulf Coast has been suffering from long-term drought, and a significant deluge is required to break it. In southern Louisiana, NOAA’s latest Drought Termination and Amelioration map (Fig. 3) shows that southern Louisiana needs 7-11 inches of rain in just one month to bring it out of long-term drought; the Florida panhandle needs about 14 inches. The place that REALLY needs the rain is the Florida peninsula, where 22-25 inches of rain is needed in one month to break its long-term drought. Unfortunately, rains are predicted to miss the Florida peninsula; less than an inch of rain is currently forecast for it over the next seven days.
Florida has received rain from the tropical system’s rainbands, but it is not enough to dent the deficit. Across west-central Florida, as highlighted by Bob Henson during his weekend coverage of Tropical Depression Two, rainfall totals ranged from 1 to 3 inches in Sarasota and Venice, while three-day totals just west of St. Petersburg reached between 6 and 7 inches.
As future Bertha slowly moves away, rain bands will gradually diminish across the Florida Peninsula. However, heavier clusters of rain are expected to spread into the Florida Panhandle, along the Alabama and Mississippi coasts, and into southern Louisiana.
Is it unusual for a storm to move westward across the Gulf?
As long as the atmospheric pattern supports it, tropical cyclones can move in directions that may seem unusual. For a westward motion like this to occur (as opposed to the more common northwestward paths), there is typically a strong subtropical ridge positioned north of the storm. This ridge blocks the cyclone from making its natural turn northward while steering currents remain weak, forcing the system farther west.
Once it gets named, Tropical Storm Bertha will join a relatively short list of storms that have formed over the eastern Gulf of Mexico and moved westward. Tropical Storm Fernand in 2019 was one of the most recent examples. Although it did not actually form in the eastern Gulf, it followed a similar westward track before making landfall in northeastern Mexico on September 4, 2019.
An even more comparable track was Hurricane Erika in 2003, which crossed much of the Gulf from east to west. Erika formed on August 14 from the remnants of a frontal boundary, strengthened into a hurricane on August 15, and made landfall near Tamaulipas, Mexico, on August 16 as a Category 1 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 75 mph (120 km/h).
Jeff Masters and Bob Henson contributed to this post.

WEATHER WATCH: Unorganized tropical depression creeps toward Louisiana
Published 9:52 am Monday, July 20, 2026
A tropical depression in the Gulf is moving slowly northwest but is expected to approach the Louisiana coastline by Wednesday, according to the National Weather Service Lake Charles.
Storm Warning Coordinator Doug Cramer says the system is not yet well-organized, with most of its rotation sitting high in the atmosphere. As of Monday morning, the depression had maximum sustained winds of 35 mph and was located 110 miles south of Panama City, Fla.
“I’ve got the satellite up and there’s some pretty good circulation across the eastern part of the Gulf of America,” Cramer said. “Most of that circulation is in the upper levels so it’s starting out as kind of like an upper-level trough and that low pressure is starting to make its way down to the surface so it’s not super organized by any means.”
What’s important to note, Cramer said, is the storm is dealing with a lot of dry air pulling in from Georgia and the Florida Panhandle.
“That dry air is starting to make its way into the storm so that’s somewhat of a positive in terms of rapid potential orientation because that dry air is going to kind of slow down the evolution of the storm a little bit,” he said.
Cramer said hurricanes feed off of moisture and humid air so the “chance for rapid intensification appears to be very low at this point, at least right now.”
The potential track for this tropical depression does include a route to Louisiana.
“The storm is moving very slow — one mile per hour to the northwest, although it is expected to pick up speed over the next four to five days as it approaches the north Gulf and the coastal areas of Mississippi and Louisiana, potentially approaching the southeast Louisiana coastline sometime Wednesday morning and then move a little bit closer to Morgan City in south central Louisiana. Maybe Vermillion Bay sometime Thursday morning and then moving off into southeast Texas potentially by Friday morning.”
If the depression does become a storm, it will be named Bertha, the second named storm of the Atlantic hurricane season.
“There is going to be the potential for good rainfall amounts, more likely on Wednesday into Thursday for Lake Charles, Alexandria and southeast Texas,” Cramer said. “If the storm takes a little more of a southern track in this cone of uncertainty and it stays offshore there could be the potential for some strong winds and the potential for storm surge. But if it makes it way inland early on and it stays on shore, then that would lessen the risk for some surge.”
While potential exists for tornadoes, it’s too early to determine that risk.

What is a tropical wave?

sources.news_title: Ask the Meteorologist: How does current storm in the Gulf differ from Bertha of 1996?
sources.text:
Tropical Depression Two is currently swirling in the northern Gulf, and it is likely to become Tropical Storm Bertha at some point Monday.
Other WRAL Top Stories
Long-time North Carolinians may remember Bertha of 1996. You might be asking, "How do we get a storm with the same name?"
Storm names are selected by the World Meteorological Organization and picked on a six-year cycle. So, the name Bertha will show up again in 2032.
Names get retired when a storm is especially damaging or deadly (see Helene, Michael, Florence, Katrina, etc.).
Hurricane Bertha 30 years ago
Bertha of 1996 was a memorable storm for North Carolina, only to be overshadowed by Hurricane Fran months later.
The storm started as a tropical wave off the coast of Africa before traveling across the Atlantic. At its peak, it was a Category 3 storm. Once it made landfall in North Carolina, it was a Category 2 hurricane.
The highest rain totals in the state was in Southport, and a 108-mph wind gust was recorded at the New River Marine Corps station. Estimated damage ranges between $270 million and $400 million, while also claiming the lives of a dozen people.
Locally, the storm produced some fairly high rain totals. That was especially the case in areas closer to I-95, thanks to the storms direct track through the eastern half of the state.
What's different about soon-to-be-Bertha in 2026?
Simply put, the storm that will likely become Bertha is not a direct hit on North Carolina. I'll post its path again.
This is a homegrown storm, in the sense that low pressure has developed off the Gulf Coast of Florida. There is nothing to grab it and pull it north. Rather, high pressure directly north of the storm will force it to retrograde (move east to west) in the coming days.
This will bring the potential for flooding rain to the Gulf states, while supplying us with distant moisture.
That will meet with a stalled front and will lead to an increase in storm chances this week.

BY MIRABEL ODETA
Tropical Depression Two formed off Florida’s west coast on Sunday morning and is forecast to strengthen into Tropical Storm Bertha within the next one to two days as the system continues to organize, forecasters said.
A Tropical Storm Watch has been issued for much of the Florida Panhandle coastline, stretching from the Ochlockonee River westward to the Alabama border, where tropical storm conditions are possible within the next 36 to 48 hours. Forecasters said additional watches or warnings could be issued farther west over the coming days depending on the system’s track and intensity.
For the Tampa Bay area, forecasters said little has changed in the local outlook. The depression is expected to continue moving away from Florida’s west coast, reducing the likelihood of significant impacts across the region.
The primary concern for the Tampa Bay area remains periods of showers and thunderstorms, with elevated rain chances expected to continue into early next week before gradually decreasing as the system moves farther away. While locally heavy rainfall is possible at times, forecasters said widespread impacts are not currently anticipated.
Additional Hurricane Hunter reconnaissance flights scheduled for Sunday afternoon are expected to provide a better assessment of the depression’s structure and overall organization, helping forecasters refine the track and intensity forecast.
Forecasters cautioned that confidence in the forecast decreases after the next 48 hours. If the center of the system remains close to the northern Gulf Coast, interaction with land and intrusions of drier air into the circulation would likely limit strengthening, favoring a weaker system tracking toward eastern Louisiana.
However, if the center stays farther offshore over the open, exceptionally warm waters of the Gulf, the depression would have a greater opportunity to organize and intensify, with the potential to reach hurricane strength. Forecasters said the distance between the center of the storm and the coastline over the next several days will play a key role in determining both its eventual strength and its track.
Meteorologists said the forecast for the Tampa Bay area has remained largely unchanged despite ongoing uncertainty about the system’s future intensity. They said the greatest question is how much strengthening occurs after the system moves away from Florida, with its development expected to depend on the balance between favorable conditions over warm Gulf waters and limiting factors such as dry air and land interaction.

Tropical Storm Bertha is headed for the Louisiana coast, as forecasters expect the storm to come ashore in the next day and bring strong winds, some coastal flooding and some storms to the southeastern portion of the state.
After becoming the second named storm of the Atlantic hurricane season overnight, Bertha strengthened Tuesday morning to speeds of 60 mph as it moved northwest through the Gulf. It is expected to make landfall as a tropical storm near Plaquemines Parish by Wednesday afternoon, forecasters with the National Hurricane Center said.
Bertha is forecast to bring gusty winds to the New Orleans area as early as Tuesday evening. Parts of southeast Louisiana could see minor to moderate storm surge flooding, and a few storms could bring heavy rain and localized flash flooding to urban areas, according to the National Weather Service’s New Orleans office.
Forecasters expect the bulk of the rainfall and wind to occur to the south of the storm’s center, thanks to the wind shear impacting the storm and giving it an asymmetrical shape.
“This should keep the greatest impact across the Gulf, but will also mean that if the storm tracks farther north, some of the more impactful weather will move onshore,” Christopher Bannan, an NWS meteorologist, said.
Timing
As of 1 p.m. Tuesday, Bertha was about 90 miles southwest of Panama City, Florida and 125 miles southeast of Mobile, Alabama. It was traveling northwest at 5 mph and producing maximum sustained winds of 60 mph.
Little additional strengthening is expected Tuesday before shear impacts weaken Bertha ahead of Wednesday landfall. Bertha should be back to maximum sustained winds of 50 mph by Wednesday morning and further drop to 40 mph by Thursday morning.
“As it gets closer to us here in southeast Louisiana, it’s going to encounter some pretty significant northeasterly wind shear,” NOLA.com senior meteorologist Damon Singleton said. “I suspect that that windshear is going to keep all of the convection to the south of us here in southeast Louisiana.”
Bertha should be in the southeastern coastal waters near Louisiana by sunrise Wednesday and move onshore in lower Plaquemines Parish in the afternoon, sometime after 1 p.m. or into the evening.

sources.news_title: Dangerous Tropical Storm Warning Issued for Alabama, Mississippi, and the Florida Panhandle
sources.text:
Tropical Storm Warnings are in effect for Gulf of America waters off Alabama, Mississippi and the Florida Panhandle beginning early Tuesday morning, with the National Weather Service warning that southwest winds gusting as high as 55 mph and seas building to 16 feet could capsize or damage vessels through Wednesday afternoon.
Pensacola to Pascagoula: New Warning Issued Monday Afternoon
The NWS Mobile office issued a new Tropical Storm Warning at 3:57 PM CDT Monday for Gulf waters from Pensacola, Florida to Pascagoula, Mississippi, and from the Okaloosa-Walton County line to Pensacola, both 20 to 60 nautical miles offshore. Forecasters expect southwest winds of 30 to 40 knots with gusts up to 55 knots and seas of 10 to 15 feet, with tropical storm force winds possible from early Tuesday morning through Wednesday afternoon.
The office was blunt about the danger to boaters: tropical storm force winds and hazardous seas will capsize or damage vessels and reduce visibility across the warned area.
Florida Panhandle Waters: Warning Remains in Effect
The NWS Tallahassee office is continuing a Tropical Storm Warning for waters from Mexico Beach to the Okaloosa-Walton County line, from Apalachicola to Mexico Beach, and from the Suwannee River to Apalachicola — all 20 to 60 nautical miles offshore. Conditions there call for southwest winds of 20 to 30 knots with gusts up to 45 knots and seas of 7 to 12 feet, with tropical storm force winds possible until early Wednesday morning. Mariners in these waters face the same capsizing and visibility hazards as those farther west.
Offshore Forecast: Seas Building to 16 Feet Tuesday Night
The National Hurricane Center‘s offshore waters forecast shows conditions deteriorating steadily through Tuesday. In the north-central Gulf, southwest to west winds are expected to reach 35 to 45 knots Tuesday night with seas of 10 to 15 feet. In the northeastern Gulf north of 26N and east of 87W, forecasters expect winds of 35 to 40 knots Tuesday night, becoming south to southwest 25 to 30 knots late, with seas building to 10 to 16 feet — the roughest conditions of the event. Numerous showers and scattered thunderstorms are expected to accompany the wind and seas through Wednesday.
Conditions are forecast to ease notably by Thursday, with winds dropping into the 10-to-20-knot range and seas falling to 5 to 7 feet as the system moves off, continuing to calm through the weekend.
What Mariners Should Do
The National Weather Service is urging anyone with plans on the water this week to change them. Mariners should alter plans to avoid these hazardous conditions — remain in port, seek safe harbor, alter course, or secure the vessel for severe conditions before tropical storm force winds arrive early Tuesday morning. Boaters should monitor the latest marine forecasts at weather.gov/mob and weather.gov/tae.

sources.news_title: Watches Expand as Tropical Storm Bertha Takes Shape
sources.text:
Tropical Depression #2 continues to drift about erratically in the northern Gulf of America and the National Hurricane Center still expects the system to develop into Tropical Storm Bertha, the second named storm of the 2026 Atlantic Hurricane Season. With the system expected to develop more and approach the coast, more advisories have been issued by the National Hurricane Center there.
Now, a Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for the area stretching from the Ochlockonee River west to the Jefferson / Plaquemines Parish border in Louisiana. A Storm Surge Watch is also now in effect for the area between the Alabama/Florida border to the Mouth of the Mississippi River. A Storm Surge Watch means there is a possibility of life-threatening inundation, from rising water moving inland from the coastline, in the indicated locations during the next 48 hours while a Tropical Storm Watch means that tropical storm conditions are possible within the watch area, in this case in the next 24 to 48 hours.
“Additional watches or warnings may be required tonight or on Tuesday,” cautions the National Hurricane Center (NHC) in their latest advisory.
The tropical depression is in light steering currents between two mid-level ridges, one to its northwest centered over the central U. S. and one to its southeast centered near the Bahamas. The U. S. ridge is expected to become a little more dominant of a steering feature as it builds eastward. The NHC expects that the cyclone will move slowly northwestward to west-northwestward for 36 hours or so, followed by a turn toward the west.
“It should be noted that strong northeasterly shear is forecast over the cyclone, which could keep the center south of the forecast track due to the effects of convective bursts. However, there are models such as the ECMWF and Canadian that bring the system inland on the northern Gulf coast,” says the NHC.
The depression is experiencing moderate northeasterly shear, and these conditions should continue for another 18-24 hours.
“It is likely that there will be convective bursts near and south of the center during this time, and these should help intensify the cyclone to a tropical storm. After that, the northeasterly shear should increase, and the global models suggest it will get strong enough to destroy the vertical integrity of the cyclone,” says the NHC. This should halt intensification and then cause weakening.
The NHC also suggests that much of the rain associated with this storm should fall over the open waters of the Gulf of America moreso than land. In their latest advisory, the NHC wrote, “It should be noted that the aforementioned shear is likely to give the cyclone a very asymmetric structure, with the bulk of the rainfall and much of the wind expected to occur to the south of the
center.”
The official storm track forecast from the National Hurricane Center brings the system through the Houston, Texas metro area by Friday afternoon as a tropical depression.

sources.news_title: Tropical Depression Two may target Texas coast by midweek
sources.text:
Tropical Depression Two may target Texas coast by midweek
A developing tropical system in the Gulf of Mexico could bring heavy rain and dangerous conditions to the Texas coast later this week, though forecasters say uncertainty about the storm’s exact path remains higher than normal.
The National Hurricane Center began issuing advisories on Tropical Depression Two over the weekend. The system is forecast to strengthen into Tropical Storm Bertha on Monday as it moves through the northeastern and north-central Gulf, according to NOAA. Early watches are confined to the Florida Panhandle, but modeling shows a sharp westward turn by late Tuesday into Wednesday that would bring the storm toward southeast Texas by Thursday or Friday.
Tropical storm-force winds could reach Texas coastal waters as early as Wednesday evening, weather officials said. Rain and thunderstorm chances are expected to increase substantially across southeast Texas on Thursday and Friday. The system is already driving a high probability of dangerous rip currents across the Gulf, according to NOAA.
Hurricane Hunter aircraft flew into the system Sunday to gather atmospheric data, with another flight planned for Monday. State and local emergency management agencies are urging residents along the upper Texas coast to monitor the storm’s progress at hurricanes.gov.

sources.news_title: Tropical Depression 2 trying to make the best of a challenging environment in the Gulf
sources.text:
In brief: TD 2 is a sloppy looking system in the Gulf, and while we should keep an eye on things, it does not appear as if this will deliver significant impacts to the Gulf Coast. We explain what’s at play here. We also take a look at a localized but notable flash flooding risk in New Jersey and NYC tomorrow.
First of all, thank you to all the new subscribers we’ve picked up in the last 24 hours. Thanks for joining us here. Our bread and butter is daily tropical weather discussions, but we also chime in on other significant weather as well. Eric is based in Houston, where I was for the last 14 years, and I am now based in southern New England. Together, we’ll keep you covered through hurricane season and beyond.
Let’s get down to business.
Tropical Depression 2 formed yesterday in the eastern Gulf. Over the next couple days, it’s expected to drift westward, becoming a tropical storm, possibly as soon as today. The satellite image of TD 2 this morning is far from impressive.
That’s basically a half-cyclone right now. That hasn’t stopped systems from becoming technically tropical or storms or hurricanes, but it does speak to limitations that they will face. In this case, both shear and dry air are going to play a major role in capping TD 2 at mid-tropical storm intensity at best I believe.
If you’re looking for a beefier tropical system, you want to see a lot less dry air than the model above shows. So right away, TD 2 is going to have to deal with continued dry air. This is not something that will change much between now and the end of TD 2’s life cycle. Additionally, while TD 2 is over warm water and dealing with minimal wind shear right now, that’s going to pick up significantly in the coming days. It’s likely that the eastern side of the storm gets blasted by northeasterly wind shear tomorrow or Wednesday, which should further limit development.
And the vast majority of tropical modeling, as well as Google Deep Mind’s 1,000 member forecast ensemble keep TD 2’s intensity at or below middle grade tropical storm levels. Interestingly, if you look at the various ensembles, you also see a lot of them “losing” Tropical Depression 2 before it gets to Texas.
In other words, we are seeing the bulk of the modeling say that TD 2 is going to run its course before getting to Lafayette or Lake Charles. The 5 to 10 percent or so that survive west of Louisiana are the ones coming to Texas. So it may look as if the modeling is all pointed right at Texas, but in reality, that’s mainly saying the remnant is. And when you look at the NHC forecast at the top, you’ll notice the intensity is dropped to depression when it makes it to Texas. Frankly, that may be generous given what we see this morning. It may be that this system ends up arriving as a shell of itself in Texas.
So what will TD 2 do? Assuming it does indeed become a tropical storm by tomorrow, we would probably see a bit of gusty wind on the coast of the Florida Panhandle, along with rain today and tomorrow. Winds as I write this are not gusting much beyond 20 mph there, however. As the system tracks to the west and as the northeasterly wind shear kicks in, most of the rain from TD 2 will migrate over the open Gulf waters.
You can see above how the bigger totals of 5 to 10 inches remain way offshore. The heaviest on land rain is likely to be today into tomorrow for the Florida Panhandle and perhaps in Plaquemines Parish, Louisiana, near where TD 2 will make a close pass Wednesday evening. Some localized flash flooding is possible, but overall this looks like a relatively gentle impact to most portions of the Gulf Coast.
There are still a handful of model ensemble members that track the system a little farther south, a scenario we discussed yesterday and still won’t completely take off the table. It’s becoming highly unlikely though. And even in those cases, it’s likely that the intensity of TD 2, or Bertha, would be capped by the aforementioned wind shear and dry air, and currently about 6 of the 1,000 Google Deep Mind ensemble members bring the storm to hurricane intensity. This was around 100 or so yesterday if I recall correctly.
So for the Florida Panhandle through Mobile, expect heavy rain and some locally gusty winds, perhaps to tropical storm force on the immediate coast. From Mobile through New Orleans, you’ll see some occasional downpours and perhaps breezy conditions but not much else. South of New Orleans through Acadiana could see some heavy rains midweek, along with breezy conditions. From Acadiana through Texas, impacts should be minimal and mostly confined to some hotter temperatures Wednesday as that northeast flow kicks in, as well as perhaps a slight chance of showers by Friday. We do not expect flooding concerns to renew in Texas.
That’s as of right this moment. Forecasts can and do change, and we encourage you to continue monitoring the forecast as the week progresses. But we do not expect a dramatic change in TD 2’s outlook right now.
Elsewhere, the Atlantic is quiet!
Northeast/Mid-Atlantic storms & flooding
Another round of storms and potential flooding returns to the East Coast tomorrow, and I am cautiously watching the corridor between Philly and New York City for flooding risks. The area is under a slight risk (level 2/4) for flash flooding, but that does not currently include New York City.
Some of the higher resolution model guidance is perking up about potential flash flooding north of I-195 in New Jersey. Flash flood guidance, or the amount of rain needed in 6 hours to trigger flash flooding is around 1 to 1.5 inches in urban northern New Jersey.
Depending on exactly how things set up tomorrow, it is possible that the flash flooding risk is a bit higher than currently presumed, particularly in the New York City metro area. Just something to pay attention to in that area.
In addition to flooding, there is an enhanced risk of severe weather, level 3/5 in areas west of I-95 tomorrow and a slight risk (2/5) elsewhere. Severe watches are likely on Tuesday as well.

sources.text:
In brief: Tropical Depression 2 may become a tropical storm later today or tomorrow, but for Houston at this point we are not expecting significant impacts, anticipating that it will fall apart before arriving here. Still, we encourage folks to monitor the forecast over the next couple days in case anything should change. Otherwise, heat is the story this week, with a legitimate shot at 100 degrees, especially Wednesday.
Tropical Depression 2
Let’s get right down to business.
Tropical Depression 2 formed yesterday in the eastern Gulf. Over the next couple days, it’s expected to drift westward, becoming a tropical storm. Now, I’ll be the first to tell you that looking at this thing on satellite this morning, it’s not exactly looking healthy.
And, in fact, the vast majority of tropical modeling, as well as Google Deep Mind’s 1,000 member forecast ensemble keep TD 2’s intensity at or below middle grade tropical storm levels. In other words, we do not believe this is going to be a repeat of Beryl. Interestingly, if you look at the various ensembles, you also see a lot of them “losing” Tropical Depression 2 before it gets to Texas.
In other words, we are seeing the bulk of the modeling say that TD 2 is going to run its course before getting to Texas. The 5 to 10 percent or so that survive west of Louisiana are the ones coming to Texas. So it may look as if the modeling is all pointed right at Texas, but in reality, that’s mainly saying the remnant is. And when you look at the NHC forecast at the top, you’ll notice the intensity is dropped to depression when it makes it to Texas. Frankly, that may be generous given what we see this morning. It may be that this system ends up arriving as a shell of itself in Texas.
There are still a handful of model ensembles that track the system a little farther south, a scenario we won’t take off the table. But in those cases, it’s likely that the intensity of TD 2, or Bertha, would be capped by wind shear. And if that doesn’t do it, dry air that surrounds this thing on all sides probably will.
So what does it mean here in Houston?
As of today, impacts are expected to be minimal. Wind impacts at this point would be tropical depression or less. Marine impacts would be for some minor coastal flooding perhaps or just slightly higher tides. And rainfall impacts would also be minimal, with just a slightly increased chance of showers on Thursday or Friday perhaps.
That’s as of right this moment. Forecasts can and do change, and we encourage you to continue monitoring the forecast as the week progresses. If something notable changes this afternoon, we’ll chime in later today.
Hottest week of summer
Meanwhile, truthfully, the bigger story this week will be the heat. This is going to be our hottest week of summer so far. We have our best chance at 100 degrees beginning tomorrow and perhaps more likely on Wednesday.
We encourage folks to try not to go out exercising during the peak heat of the day, drink water, and just keep in mind that while your body adapts to summer heat, some days are just a little bit worse than others. That’s Tuesday and especially Wednesday. On the flip side, the humidity doesn’t look overly impressive. In fact, because of Tropical Depression 2, Houston may actually see some drier air filter in out of the northeast. That won’t make it feel gloriously comfortable, but it may allow for heat index values (or “real feel” temperatures) to be somewhat tolerable. It may also mean the difference between a heat advisory instead of an extreme heat warning.
After Friday
As noted earlier, the remnants of TD 2 could provide a slight bump in shower chances Thursday or Friday. After that, it looks like very standard summer here. We’ll probably have a couple thunderstorms each day but nothing significant. Temperatures will be hot but not extreme. And barring any change in pattern, it should be fairly calm.

sources.news_title: Bryan Norcross: Tropical depression is struggling but Bertha is still forecast to develop in the Northern Gulf
sources.text:
Bryan Norcross: Tropical depression is struggling but Bertha is still forecast to develop in the Northern Gulf
The overall environment is less conducive to organizing and strengthening today, but the moderately hostile upper winds still might abate enough for the system to spin up into Tropical Storm Bertha.
Last updated at 9:15 a.m. on Monday, July 20, 2026
Tropical Depression Two has a broad circulation with clusters of heavy thunderstorms, but it's infused with dry air. The overall environment is less conducive to organizing and strengthening today, but the moderately hostile upper winds still might abate enough for the system to spin up into Tropical Storm Bertha. So far, the sustained winds are less than 40 mph.
Rain bands rotating around the sprawling circulation contain tropical downpours. In the short term, rainfall will be the biggest threat wherever they spread over the coastal sections.
Onshore wind in Apalachee Bay south of Tallahassee could push the water 1 to 3 feet above the normal high tide level. As the storm tracks west, watch for elevated tides all along the northern Gulf Coast.
For the next couple days, the system will drift northwest to west offshore of the coastline. The expectation is for a slow strengthening process under slightly less hostile upper winds, so that by later today or tomorrow, the depression will strengthen enough for the National Hurricane Center to upgrade it to Tropical Storm Bertha.
Remember the rule: Predictions for just-developing, poorly developed, and slow-moving systems are subject to much higher errors, and forecast details are likely to change. Every caveat applies to this system.
Yesterday, there was some concern that Bertha might develop quickly and miss interaction with land as it moved to the west later in the week. That might have resulted in a stronger system reaching Texas. But today, the strong consensus of the computer forecasts is that the depression or a weak Bertha will run into Louisiana and die out there.
The yellow line represents the consensus of the traditional models, and the red one is the Google DeepMind forecast. Notice that both of them lose the circulation over Louisiana.
In addition, upper-level winds are forecast to be quite hostile at that point. Those winds would likely carry the moisture from what's left of the depression or Bertha toward Texas.
Until or if a well-developed center actually forms, the forecasts will be iffy. But the trends are good for a low-end tropical storm at most.
Those upper-level winds are also likely to push the heaviest rain south of the coast and over the Gulf. But heavy, tropical rain bands with gusty winds are still possible at the coast and in adjacent inland sections. Be ready for any local alerts from the National Weather Service.
For now, there's nothing to do but stay aware. We have to see how the system develops today. Will the hostile environment of upper-level winds and dry air continue to take its toll, or will a pocket of conducive atmosphere allow the system to become better developed? Forecasts for well-organized systems are almost always more accurate.

Those areas along the northern Gulf Coast were under a tropical storm warning through Wednesday and could see heavy rain and flooding into Thursday morning, the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said Tuesday. New Orleans was under a tropical storm watch.

We won’t be seeing any impacts from this second storm of the season, but if you have plans along the gulf coast this week plan for at least some rain and winds.
